desc:
Split nums into two non-empty contiguous parts left and right (a prefix and the remaining suffix) such that every element of left is less than or equal to every element of right. Return the smallest possible length of left.

nums = [5, 0, 3, 8, 6]
result = 3     (left = [5, 0, 3], right = [8, 6])
nums = [1, 1, 1, 0, 6, 12]
result = 4

The input is guaranteed to admit at least one valid split.
constraints: At least one valid split exists
hints: Checking each split point with a fresh max of the prefix and min of the suffix costs O(n<sup>2</sup>). Precompute them.
A split after index i is valid exactly when max(nums[0..i]) ≤ min(nums[i+1..n-1]). Build a suffix-minimum array and sweep with a running prefix maximum.

For O(1) extra space keep two values while sweeping: leftMax (maximum of the current left part) and seenMax (maximum of everything scanned). If a new element is smaller than leftMax, it must join the left part: extend the left part to it and set leftMax = seenMax.
editorial: Suffix minima approach: compute sufMin[i] = min(nums[i:]) and scan left to right with the running prefix maximum; the first i with prefMax(i) ≤ sufMin[i + 1] gives the answer i + 1. This is O(n) time and O(n) space.

The two-pointer version starts with the left part equal to [nums[0]]. Scanning the remaining elements, any element smaller than the current left maximum cannot be in the right part, so the left part must grow to include it, and then the maximum of the left part becomes the largest value seen so far (including those just swallowed). Elements not smaller than leftMax just update seenMax.
A single pass: O(n) time, O(1) extra space. Equal values are allowed on both sides, which is why the comparison with leftMax is strict.
